newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela Cenbank mega-bond key to stability.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela Cenbank mega-bond key to stability.

text.p: Venezuela's approval of a $3.94 billion mega-bond to be issued by the Finance Ministry to pay off long-standing government debts with the Central Bank is a crucial step forward for the country's economic stabilization program, analysts said.

"If the government keeps to its agreement with the Central Bank ... greater monetary stability in the short and medium-term will be practically assured," VenEconomy analyst Jose Juan Gomes said in a recent article.

Under the scheme, approved by congress Wednesday, the dollar- denominated mega-bond will be issued directly to the Central Bank, effectively rescheduling the government's $3.94 billion debt at market interest rates.
The debts, made up of $3.7 billion and 113 billion bolivars ($240 million), stem from the early 1990s when the Central Bank put up collateral for the country's Brady debt restructuring.

The Central Bank will then issue bolivar-denominated paper on behalf of the Treasury at the rate of 0.75 percent of Gross Domestic Product per year (roughly 220 billion bolivars or $470 million) to pay interest and principal on the bond.
Amortization is expected over 18 years.
The arrangement has a number of benefits, analysts said.
First, it is expected to put the Central Bank's balance sheet back in the black after a 45 billion bolivar ($96 million) loss for the first half of 1996.
That loss was due to an asymmetry between low-yielding Central Bank assets, such as government debt, and expensive liabilities, such as the Central Bank's monetary stabilization notes, known as TEMs.
TEMS are short term bonds backed by the Central Bank and used to conduct open market operations.
"The Bank was technically bankrupt ... but this mega-bond will help it's balance sheet," congressman Juan Sosa Maury of the Convergencia party told Reuters.
Second, the bolivar-denominated Treasury bills issued by the government to pay off the bond will add a monetary policy weapon to the Central Bank's limited arsenal.
Currently, the Central Bank only uses TEMs to conduct open market operations. Henceforth the Treasury bills will be issued alongside TEM paper.
"The Central Bank will issue the Treasury bills to mop up liquidity, substituting for TEMs as an instrument of monetary policy," Maury said.

Third, although TEMs are expected to continue as a benchmark for wider interest rates, the shift towards the use of Treasury bills in open market operations "is by no means a trivial difference from the point of view of monetary policy," said Gomes.

Analysts say the Central Bank's reliance on TEMs to soak up liquidity has produced a debt snowball. The financing costs of each TEM issue have to be met with another TEM issue, whose costs in turn have to be met with another issue, and so on.
Instead of reducing liquidity, TEMs actually increase financial liquidity over the long term, runs the argument.
By contrast, when "the Treasury foots the bill liquidity contracts because it is forced either to reduce spending or increase revenue (i.e. raise taxes) to meet its commitments," said Gomes.
A potential side effect of the mega-bond is that its dollar- denomination would increase the fiscal cost of any large devaluation.

As Venezuela exports upwards of $16 billion of oil each year, devaluations boost government revenues in bolivar terms. That makes devaluing a tempting recourse if there is a yawning fiscal deficit to close.

But "by partially removing one of the fiscal benefits to devaluation, the move suggests the authorities are truly committed to reforming the fiscal accounts... and maintaining a strong bolivar," said New York based IDEA analyst Gene Freida.
-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600
